The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook; however, evidence from the credit-channel literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist) suggests that the Federal Reserve’s rapid move to the effective lower bound, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanded repo operations, discount-window easing, and dollar swap lines can stabilize funding markets by lowering external finance premia and supporting spending and investment. Consistent with frameworks that emphasize expectations and the Taylor principle—as well as inflation-forecast targeting insights—anchoring longer-term inflation expectations (even as market-based inflation compensation falls) increases the likelihood that these actions cushion real activity, including in a potential liquidity-trap environment where nontraditional tools become pivotal.
